extracted.intended_audience: educated general readers / subscribers of The Spectator (early 18th-century periodical audience)
extracted.subtask_description: Expository and moralizing essays and letters on subjects like perception of time, mourning, servants, duels, and women's dress, aimed at instructing and entertaining a general early-18th-century readership.

rubrics_metrics.name: Perception of Time (Duration) via succession of ideas
rubrics_metrics.description: Our Notion of Time is produced by reflecting on the Succession of Ideas in our Mind; the Succession may be infinitely accelerated or retarded, so different Beings may have different Notions of the same Parts of Duration (Locke / Malebranche viewpoint).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Implication / application given: 'The Hours of a wise Man are lengthened by his Ideas' — by employing Thoughts on many Subjects or entertaining a quick and constant Succession of Ideas one 'lengthens' life; conversely thinking on nothing shortens Time. Example/anti‑pattern: sleeping without dreaming gives no Perception of Time; fixing thought on a single idea makes Time seem shorter.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sincerity of Grief vs outward demonstrations
rubrics_metrics.description: Outward signs (tears, facial gestures) are fallacious measures of true Affliction; 'true Affliction labours to be invisible, ... is a Stranger to Ceremony, and ... bears in its own Nature a Dignity much above the little Circumstances which are affected under the Notion of Decency.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Guidance to critics/observers: do not judge depth of sorrow by visible weeping—children and certain constitutions shed tears easily; deep sorrow may 'stop all the Passages for Tears'. Anti‑pattern: assuming a person who 'wants that Quantity of Salt-water' is insensible; measuring friendship by quantity of tears is unreliable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appropriate aims for female education / improvement
rubrics_metrics.description: Women should 'improve in our own Sphere, and approve our selves better Daughters, Wives, Mothers, and Friends' rather than merely becoming scholars for show; modest extension: a little philosophy to subdue passions and study of arithmetic is recommended.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical advice: prefer instructive works (e.g., Bishop of Cambray's 'Education of a Daughter') that teach principles of justice, gratitude, sincerity, prudence, modesty; study arithmetic as useful; caution against making the sex scholars merely to mirror men's accomplishments—education should be fitted to social/functioning roles.

rubrics_metrics.name: Judging servants by context and example of superiors
rubrics_metrics.description: Servants are not inherently rogues; their behaviour reflects the Example and Mode of living set by their Superiors (wages, manner of living, and treatment shape servants' conduct).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluation guidance: when assessing servants' virtue or vice, consider their upbringing and the example of masters; the letter traces how varied employments and masters produced very different behaviour—anti‑pattern is a sweeping condemnation of all servants.

rubrics_metrics.name: Public policy and moral rationale against duels
rubrics_metrics.description: Duels are a custom that 'in contempt of all Laws Divine and Human' have made 'Forgiveness of Injuries' vile; they invert rules of good society and make the daring of death an honour—thus warranting strong measures to 'blot this Fashion' by law.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Legislative/disciplinary prescriptions in the edict: those who send or accept challenges shall be incapable of bearing office; personal estate to the successful claimant; real estate vested in next heir; no royal pardons for such offences. Rationale: use legal incapacitation, loss of estate and honour, and social shame rather than torture; mercy to particulars can be cruelty in the general (policy principle).

rubrics_metrics.name: Reasoned punishment vs spectacle or torture
rubrics_metrics.description: When reforming a social custom (e.g., duelling), punishments should be proportionate and directed to change the mode rather than to 'put Human Nature ... to Disgrace' by tortures; public ignominy, loss of civil rights and estate are proposed instead.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Policy guidance: prefer measures that alter incentives and social regard (incapacity for office, forfeiture) over cruel punishments; acknowledge exceptions where laws already provide remedies and allow some particular cases to be handled within existing law.

rubrics_metrics.name: Aesthetic principle: head-dress should not exceed nature's symmetry
rubrics_metrics.description: Women should not add 'any thing that can be ornamental to what is already the Master-piece of Nature.' Excessive head-dress destroys the symmetry of the human figure and calls off the eye from 'great and real Beauties' to 'childish Gewgaws'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Fashion guidance: recommend modesty and proportion in coiffure; praise current reduction of excessive height in head-dresses; anti‑pattern: extravagant 'Fontanges' or towering constructions that make a woman appear 'a Colossus' and distract from the face's natural features.
